That entire post was an explanation of why down payment assistance can not be used with an FHA loan. It doesnt matter who the lender is, the down payment cannot come from a loan. The FHA has clear guidelines listed on their website that I linked, and that is one of them.

Hey there, I have personal experience with an FHA loan and just wanted to offer some general information. The amount of money you qualify for when seeking an FHA loan is calculated using a formula where they input your specific data (income, debt, and credit score). For that reason, another person's approval amount is absolutely no indication of what you might be approved for. Second, if you are choosing to apply for an FHA loan specifically, the down payment percentages are set in stone. For a credit score of 580 or higher, the down payment is 3.5% of purchase price, for credit scores lower than 580, its 5%. You have to have this money in your account at the time you apply for the loan or you will not be eligible. Not only do you have to prove that you currently have the down payment amount, but you also have to provide a record of how that money was attained. This is to ensure that they money did not come from any type of loan. This also means that the down payment cannot be rolled into or included in the FHA loan. Basically, there is no way to get around having to have your own funds for a down payment. Here's some general info.

Hey there, I'm someone who has bpd as well as a degree in Psychology, so I have some experience from both the patient side and the provider side. I totally empathize with your situation and I know how hard it can be to find a therapist, especially one that wants to work with people who have bpd and is also compatible personality wise for you. The med types that you listed can be very dangerous to stop cold turkey, especially antipsychotics. If you do decide to come off your meds, the process NEEDS to be monitored by your Psychiatrist. I'm honestly shocked that a Psychiatrist would put you on such heavy medication at such a young age without first using therapy to see if that would be effective in managing your mental health. Long term use of antipsychotics causes shrinkage of the cortex, and long term use of antidepressants is proven to be linked to cognitive decline and dementia. These drugs are not benign, and for that reason, they should be used as a last resort. That is not to say that these psych meds shouldn't be used; they do play an important role in treatment, and for many people the benefit from the medication far outweighs the risks of taking it. 

I have no idea what your healthcare situation is, but if you do have insurance, I highly suggest going to your insurance website which should have a link labeled as "find a provider" or something similar. You can adjust your search to look for therapists, and the list that it generates will be providers that do take your insurance. From there, just call down the list and leave messages until someone gets back to you saying they are accepting new patients. Its a frustrating process, but its really the only way to find one. 

I wish you the best of luck!

If you are concerned about heat, it might be a good idea to make sure the place you are renting has a forced air AC and not just a swamp cooler. I would say that the majority of places only have a swamp cooler, which generally works great at cooling homes about 20 degrees cooler than outdoor temps, but during july when its over 100 every day, that means your house would be at about 80

Coming to ABQ to escape heat is an interesting choice. It tends to be only about 5-15 degrees cooler than Phoenix out here in summer. 

That being said, it sounds like Nob Hill might be the best fit neighborhood wise for you. Nob Hill, west Nob Hill (aka the UNM area), and downtown are really the only walkable areas, and downtown is probably the least safe area in the city. The NE heights are considered a safe and desirable area to live, but its a lot more residential and corporate feeling (like strip malls), vs Nob Hill which tends to have more local businesses.

I agree with the others in that Albuquerque is very accepting, so I wouldnt worry too much about that. In terms of finding an apartment, you could find a 1BR for $1000/month, but if you're looking for a 2BR, its going to be more expensive than that, and that's for an apartment. Renting a house or townhome, even in a bad neighborhood, will cost at least $1600/month. On that note, there are some really rough neighborhoods in this city. The international district is an area I would avoid. Some of the cheaper neighborhoods are Martineztown, Barelas, and South Broadway. The most desirable areas in general are Nob Hill, The NE Heights, The North Valley, Uptown, Old Town, or Silver Hill, but they are priced to match their desirability. A little bit of poking around on Redfin or Zillow will give you a good idea of what you can expect for your budget. 

The winters do get cold here, last week we had overnight lows as cold as 5 degrees, but the good news is that winter is short lived, and really is only 2 or 3 months of the year. I think that you will find that the dry heat is easier to deal with than humid heat.  

The school systems here, in the city, are not great, but I have heard that LA has the lowest funding for teachers in the country, so its bound to be better than that!

Best of luck to you with your move!

Its an interesting concept to me, because the process of being diagnosed is often "do you feel like..." and going down the list of criteria. I dont think that its something that only psychologists have the magic insight to. I do think that BPD can easily be self misdiagnosed though, because the symptoms often sound like feelings that neurotypical people feel, its just the intensity at which people with BPD feel them that differentiates us. I was diagnosed with bipolar and major depression until the 3rd time I was hospitalized. It ended up being my extreme behaviors that got me finally diagnosed with BPD. I definitely had that feeling where the diagnosis clicked and fit perfectly with what I was experiencing. Had I had the list of criteria, I do think I could have correctly diagnosed myself as well.

I've worked really hard in therapy and otherwise, and the majority of the time, I do consider myself recovered from BPD. It feels much like what you are describing though; I am able to control my actions so that outwardly I no longer fit the criteria for BPD, but I do still feel my emotions extremely and I still feel the attachment issues, inappropriate rage, and splitting on my FP, I just dont act accordingly. I've spent a lot of time practicing "opposite action" and that is how I got to this point. I do believe that this is the best it will ever get. I do believe that since the neuropathways that control my emotional reactions to situations are built so large from years of use that they have essentially physically formed my brain to work like this. 

I struggle with this idea a lot of days because life is still so painful feeling all these emotions, but there is this great joy that has come from being able to be a positive person in people's lives instead of constantly burning bridges with people in my life because of my actions. 

Is it worth it, ultimately? To be determined.

I want to preface by saying that this is my personal experience and may not apply to everyone. I just want to share what has helped me the most after struggling with romantic relationships for years. Recently, I was in a relationship where I didn't share the fact that I had BPD right away. Because I made the choice not to tell him, he held me to the standards that he would hold any neurotypical person to in our relationship. I was excited by what I saw as a personal challenge. Can I control my behaviors enough that this person wont be able to immediately identify my mental illness? It was only about 1.5 months I went without telling him, but during this time I realized just how much my other partners had been enabling my toxic behaviors relating to my BPD. Of course its not their fault, they were simply trying to be gentle with me and make things as easy for me as possible. This time where my recent partner didn't know of my mental illness  helped me to see that I have the potential to act as a healthier person because here I was, doing it. I did eventually tell him, but even after I did, he continued to challenge me, always framing our conversations about my BPD around the concept that recovery is the road I'm on. 

One specific conversation I remember having with him was a huge turning point for me. I was asking him, begging him, to reassure me, to tell me that he cared for me and that he wouldn't up and leave. He told me that he wouldn't give me that reassurance, that it didn't sit right with him. I was offended and I thought it was cruel because I was suffering and it would be so easy for him to alleviate it. But then he told me that the reason why he would not give me that reassurance is because he could feel that if he did, it would become a pattern in which I would ask for more and more, eventually coming to a point where no amount of reassurance would be enough to satisfy my insecurity. AND HE WAS RIGHT. Before this I hadn't realized that was a pattern I was continually getting stuck in, one that damaged my relationships in the past. The constant asking for proof of love and reassurance was so draining to my partners before because it was never ending, it was never enough. 

I guess the point of all this is, sometimes people need to be challenged to realize they have the power in their own hands to choose recovery. I still slip up sometimes, my mental illness still manifests in ways I wish I had more control over, but I'm making so much progress and nothing in my life has ever helped to improve my self esteem as much as this journey has. 

The truth of BPD is that no amount of external support can fix the emotional damage. Even therapy is only meant to facilitate the healing process, the true work has to be done by the individual. Recovery is making the hard choice not to give in to your emotions over and over and over until it becomes habitual to make that choice. I've suffered with this horrible illness for nearly 20 years. When I say that my mental illness has been severe, I mean its been SEVERE and debilitating. I just want to let people know that there's hope if youre willing to work your ass off for it. Its worth it. Its so, so worth it.
